title: Should Ethereum issue less ETH?
intro: A common view has been that Ethereum should issue only as much new ETH as it needs to stay secure. This map follows the argument over whether to issue less, from the first research in 2023 to EIP-8363 in 2026, in talks, research posts and forum replies. The 0.5% cap quoted from 2026 is the earlier minimum viable issuance proposal, not EIP-8363's tapered burn.

stops.author: Anders Elowsson
stops.note: The founding case for minimum viable issuance: excess issuance is an inflation tax on ordinary users and lets one LST become the money of Ethereum.

lines.text: Staking should secure Ethereum, but not become an inflation tax, degrading utility and liquidity while generating monopolistic hazard.
If the protocol does not operate under MVI, but at a higher deposit ratio, one or a few LSTs may overtake as money in the Ethereum ecosystem, embedding themselves across every layer and application.

stops.author: sacha
stops.note: First written rebuttal to MVI: lower rewards turn staking into a margins contest that scale wins.

lines.text: Practically speaking, under MVI, lower rewards will mean greater (if not exclusive) competition on margins. Economies of scale on cost will, in all likelihood, end up winning out, and bigger players will be in a position to either price out or outlast smaller ones.

stops.author: @adietrichs and @casparschwa
stops.source_title: Endgame Staking Economics: A Case for Targeting
stops.note: The opening post of the thread the map already quotes replies to: the researchers state the case that the current curve lets all ETH be staked and propose targeting a range of staking ratios.

lines.text: In short, the current issuance policy allows for all ETH to be eventually staked. This arguably over-secures the protocol and comes with negative externalities. We elaborate why the endgame of staking economics should target a staking ratio range instead. The intention is to provide enough security for the protocol, while limiting the negative externalities of too much stake in the system.

stops.author: @adietrichs and @caspar
stops.note: The concrete proposal itself: change the issuance curve in Electra, because without it the current policy stays for about two years. The thread the map quotes replies from.

lines.text: Thus, Ethereum will remain under current issuance policy for at least 9-12 months, and without a change included in Electra, it will be ~2 years.

stops.author: artofkot
stops.note: ETF-driven custody flows could give one custodian a majority of a capped staking set.

lines.text: If the staking ratio 1/4 is targeted (~30m ETH), we arrive at the very much possible scenario of Coinbase controlling 51% of staked ETH.

I think that the premise of the staking endgame (capping and targeting 1/4 level) is dangerous and may allow 51% attacks in the future, in the view of very strong institutional flows into staking market.

stops.note: Reply to the solo-staker objection: sunk costs keep existing solo stakers; the pool of future ones is mostly depleted anyway.

lines.text: Solo staking costs are mostly upfront, and current solo stakers have already paid them. It seems to me that one could reasonably expect many of them to stick around.

stops.author: sharp
stops.note: Lower issuance pushes yield-seekers into restaking, creating a new concentration risk.

lines.text: ETH holders will always seek yield, adjusting Ethereum's issuance curve with the intent of decreasing the % of staked ETH will likely push ETH holders further up the risk curve leading to higher restaking concentration on Eigenlayer.

stops.author: barnabe
stops.note: Reply to the custodian worry: at a lower yield, custodians would re-decide whether to stake, so their stake would fall.

lines.text: A new equilibrium would be found, where the share of Coinbase in the staking set would likely not simply be their custodied amount at stake under the previous configuration with non-targeting issuance curve (so 15m staked, say) divided by the target (30m).
I would expect the net effect to be a reduction of Coinbase's nominal amount of ETH at stake.

stops.author: OisinKyne
stops.note: Fix LST dominance by making native staking liquid (fast exits) instead of cutting yield.

lines.text: I'm firmly opposed to MVI as a direction, and think the impact of this change would be very negative for the health of the Ethereum network.

As a counterproposal, if the problem to be solved is LSTs becoming the base asset for the network, I think we should fix the primary downside of native staking, by allowing a mechanism for someone to exit their stake at finality for an escalating basefee.

stops.author: Draco
stops.source_title: Endgame Staking Economics: A Case for Targeting
stops.note: Targeting the stake ratio is the wrong lever; fix the structural advantages of staking providers directly.

lines.text: The dominance of SSPs (and in turn, the staking ratio issue) is a result of average ETH holders making rational economic decisions. The threat posed by SSP dominance is not a new topic and yet we have make little progress solving it. And I'd argue the reason we found ourselves in this situation because we have not been willing to address the structural advantages of SSPs over solo stakers In the end, it's an incentive problem. And it is best (can only be) fixed with incentives

stops.author: 0xemperor
stops.source_title: Endgame Staking Economics: A Case for Targeting
stops.note: Issuance is the price Ethereum pays for security; cutting it risks underpaying.

lines.text: The issuance ultimately is a value that reflects the networks' willingness to pay for its own security, which coupled with the burn has actually resulted in a negative issuance since the merge overall.

stops.author: danw.eth
stops.source_title: Endgame Staking Economics: A Case for Targeting
stops.note: Pro-reduction counterpoint from a home staker: holding ETH without yield is viable.

lines.text: I think it's a misconception that it's not viable to hold ETH without a yield. Bitcoin is held without a mining yield, and the recent ETF flows have proven that people don't need a yield to simply hold an asset.

stops.author: Valdorff
stops.note: Thin margins select for validators best at extracting value, not for those best at securing the chain.

lines.text: I think a proposal like this, if implemented, would essentially end solo staking (with the exception of some very large solo stakers, and some altruists willing to lose money for ethos).

Making staking profits marginal will ensure that the only validators left are those that are most effective at extracting value -- this is extremely different from those that are most effective at securing the chain (I would argue there's a negative correlation).

stops.note: The author of the curve the Electra proposal adopted sets out the rationale for a tempered reward curve in his own post, the longer form of a forthcoming EIP.

lines.text: The equilibrium yield offered to stakers corresponds to the cost that the marginal staker assigns to staking, i.e., their indifference point between staking and not staking. This explains why all ETH holders can benefit from an issuance reduction, something which is also illustrated in Figure 2.

stops.author: Vitalik Buterin
stops.source_title: Possible futures of the Ethereum protocol, part 3: The Scourge
stops.note: Vitalik: staking is already past what security needs, and near-universal staking turns staking into a chore handed to central operators.

lines.text: Today, about 30% of the ETH supply is actively staking. This is far more than enough to protect Ethereum from 51% attacks. If the percent of ETH staked grows much larger, researchers fear a different scenario: the risks that would arise if almost all ETH becomes staked. These risks include: Staking turns from being a profitable task for specialists into a duty for all ETH holders.

lines.text: If total staking returns drop below 0.85%, solo staking will be unviable for many people at these levels.

lines.text: The current issuance curve is a trap. Unfortunately, like Bitcoin's issuance, Ethereum's issuance was misdesigned. It guarantees 2% tail APR, even if 100% ETH is staked.

soft cap: The staking fraction where issuance returns to zero. To me a 50% staking soft cap feels credibly neutral and pragmatic.

stops.source_title: Quote post on the Ethereum Validators Association issuance debate
stops.note: Péter Szilágyi, who led Geth until 2025 and holds most of his net worth in ETH, says the debate treats a symptom: people stake because using ETH onchain is risky (what he calls the casino) and offers little else to do. Cutting rewards would push holders into that risky onchain use or out of ETH. His fix is useful apps, a more reliable ecosystem and recourse for users when things go wrong, not monetary policy.

lines.text: the reason everyone stakes ETH is because there isn't anything else to do with it!
Sure, you can shove it in the casino and hope it doesn't get drained
The entire Ether issuance discussion is trying to remedy the symptom instead of the root of the problem.
The symptom is that everyone wants to stake instead of using the network, so there's no economic activity being generated.
by reducing the issuance you're making people choose between the casino or exiting.
Improve the human condition and they will spend ETH on it and generate economic activity.
Improve the reliability of the ecosystem so people aren't afraid of losing their saving while they sleep.
People want to live their lives, not play onchain PvP against the entire world.

stops.place: EIP-8363 and its Ethereum Magicians thread
stops.title: No issuance change adopted
stops.body: EIP-8363, Tapered Issuance Burn, was withdrawn from consideration for the Hegota upgrade on 1 October 2026 by its champion Jérôme de Tychey. His post says several parties argued that fork scoping was the wrong venue for an issuance policy change, and the authors agreed. It lays out a staged process of forums and workshops from Devcon in November to EthCC in April, aiming for one draft EIP or a record of why none emerged. Replies through 31 October question that process, including its in-person forums and what counts as an in-scope objection, and some opponents restate their objections. The EIP page still lists it as a Draft. We found no adopted issuance change. Forkcast lists its Hegota status as Declined at All Core Devs Consensus #188 on 1 October 2026, where Alex Stokes announced the withdrawal.
stops.note: Primary sources, re-read 8 Nov 2026: Ethereum Magicians, EIP-8363 thread (discussions-to of the EIP), post 271 by jdetychey, 1 Oct 2026, 'Withdrawing EIP-8363 from consideration for Hegota'; later posts 272 (5 Oct), 273 (8 Oct), 274 (30 Oct) and 276 (31 Oct) raise process and substance objections; no later post found as of 8 Nov (228 posts, last 31 Oct). eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8363 (status: Draft); All Core Devs Consensus #184 (6 Aug 2026) and #188 (1 Oct 2026). The body says only what these sources say. Forkcast (public/artifacts/acdc/2026-10-01_188/eip_mentions.json) reads "withdrawn" for ACDC #188 and the EIP record labels the stage Declined.
